questions.question: What is a probability density function for a continuous random variable?
options: A function assigning positive probability to each exact value
A list of probabilities for finitely many outcomes
A rule that must be negative outside the support
A nonnegative function whose interval integrals give probabilities

questions.question: What total area must a probability density have?
How are probabilities over intervals represented by a PDF?
options: As areas under the density curve
As probabilities at the two endpoints only
As counts of all integer values in the interval

questions.question: For a continuous random variable with a density, the probability $P(X=c)$ at any single point $c$ equals:
If the CDF is differentiable, how is the density related to it?
options: The density is the derivative of the CDF
The density is the reciprocal of the CDF
The density is the CDF squared
The density is unrelated to the CDF

questions.question: Which statement describes the uniform density on an interval?
options: It is constant across that interval
It assigns mass only to integers
It is highest at zero and then decreases

questions.question: Which density is described as bell-shaped and centered at its mean?
Which density is highest at zero and decreases as waiting time grows?
If $f_X(x)=2$ on $[0,1/2]$ and $0$ elsewhere, why can this be a PDF?
options: It is invalid because a density can never exceed $1$
It is nonnegative and its total area is $1$
It is valid only if it is negative outside the interval
It gives probability $2$ to every exact point

questions.question: Using a PDF, which expression gives $P(1\le X\le 3)$?
The value $f_X(x)$ of a density at a point $x$ represents:
options: a value that must lie in $[0,1]$

questions.question: Why must a PDF be nonnegative?
options: Every density value must equal a probability
Negative density could create negative interval probabilities
Nonnegative functions always integrate to zero.

questions.question: The CDF $F_X(x)$ is obtained from the density $f_X$ by:
If $f_X(x)=1/5$ on $[0,5]$, what is $P(1\le X\le 4)$?
If $f_X(x)=2x$ on $[0,1]$, what is $P(0\le X\le 1/2)$?
If $F_X(x)=x^2$ on $0\le x\le1$ and is differentiable there, what is the density on that interval?
Can a valid PDF have a value greater than $1$ at some point?
options: No, every density value must be a probability
Only if the random variable is discrete
Yes, as long as it is nonnegative and the total area is $1$
Only when the CDF is decreasing

questions.question: If a density is higher near $2$ than near $5$, what local probability comparison is justified?
options: The point probability at $2$ is larger than the point probability at $5$.
All outcomes below $2$ are more likely than all outcomes above $5$.
The density must integrate to more than $1$ near $2$.
Comparable small intervals near $2$ carry more probability mass than near $5$.
